choices.text: A large molecule or network host binds a smaller guest molecule in a binding pocket through noncovalent interactions
A small molecule binds a larger one by forming new covalent bonds
choices.why: Host-guest binding is noncovalent, and the host is the larger partner.

choices.text: Two identical molecules form a covalent dimer
choices.why: Host and guest are different species, and they are held together by noncovalent interactions.

choices.text: A solvent dissolves a solute
choices.why: Solvation is not host-guest binding. A host binds a guest in a specific binding pocket.

explanation: In host-guest chemistry, a large molecule or network host uses noncovalent interactions to bind a smaller guest in a binding pocket. It is analogous to how antibodies bind antigens and enzymes bind substrates. A simple example is the binding of C60 by calix[5]arenes, mainly through π stacking.

prompt: Why do effective hosts tend to be rigid, preorganized structures such as macrocycles or cages?

choices.text: A floppy host loses a lot of conformational entropy when it wraps around a guest, which makes ΔS of binding more negative and disfavors binding
Rigid hosts form covalent bonds with the guest more easily
choices.why: Host-guest binding is noncovalent. Rigidity matters because it limits the entropy lost on binding.

choices.text: Flexible hosts bind too strongly to release the guest
choices.why: Flexibility weakens binding, because of the entropy lost when the host is forced into one shape.

choices.text: Rigid hosts make ΔH of binding positive
choices.why: Preorganization is about the entropy term. A rigid host has little conformational entropy to lose, so ΔS is less negative.

explanation: When a conformationally flexible host binds a guest, it conforms to the guest's shape and becomes more rigid, losing conformational entropy. That makes ΔS more negative and disfavors binding. Effective hosts limit their conformational entropy from the start by fusing binding sites into a macrocyclic ring, cage, or cluster. The more rigid, the better.

prompt: When a nonpolar host and a nonpolar guest are mixed in water, why do they tend to stick together?

choices.text: Their association frees water molecules to form water-water hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the water-solute interactions they replace
The nonpolar molecules strongly attract each other through hydrogen bonds
choices.why: Nonpolar molecules can't hydrogen bond with each other. The driving force is the stronger water-water interactions released when they associate.

choices.text: Water repels nonpolar molecules with a strong repulsive force
choices.why: As the magnetic marble analogy shows, the nonpolar parts aren't repelled. The water molecules simply attract one another more strongly.

choices.text: Nonpolar molecules react covalently in water
choices.why: No covalent bonds form. Desolvation, driven by preferential solvent-solvent interactions, brings them together.

explanation: π–π and similar interactions are weak compared with water-water hydrogen bonds. Every dipole-induced dipole or X-H π interaction between water and a solute is a lost opportunity for hydrogen bonding, so nonpolar parts of host and guest stick together, freeing water to interact with itself. The hydrophobic effect is the most prominent example.

prompt: Aromatic π systems engage in unusually strong π–π stacking interactions. What makes this possible?

choices.text: Their electron distributions are easily distorted, giving strong dispersion and dipole-induced dipole interactions
Aromatic rings form covalent bonds between stacked rings
choices.why: π stacking is a noncovalent interaction, a combination of dispersion and electrostatic interactions.

choices.text: Aromatic rings carry full positive and negative charges
choices.why: Neutral aromatic rings aren't ions. Their easily polarized π clouds give strong dispersion and dipole-induced dipole forces.

choices.text: Stacking is always electrostatically attractive, whatever the arrangement
choices.why: The electrostatic part can be attractive or repulsive. The eclipsed benzene dimer, for example, is electrostatically disfavored.

explanation: Because the electron distribution in aromatic systems is easily distorted, they engage in atypically strong dispersion and dipole-induced dipole interactions called π–π stacking. The rings stack parallel, in a sandwich or displaced arrangement. The electrostatic contribution can be attractive or repulsive, and the eclipsed benzene dimer is electrostatically disfavored.

prompt: Benzene and hexafluorobenzene form an eclipsed, face-to-face heterodimer. In the Lewis acid-base description of this pair, which ring acts as the Lewis base?

choices.text: Benzene, whose relatively electron-rich π system donates to the electron-poor hexafluorobenzene π system
Hexafluorobenzene, because fluorine atoms have lone pairs
choices.why: The electronegative F substituents make the C6F6 π system electron-poor, so C6F6 is the acceptor (Lewis acid).

choices.text: Neither, since π stacking can never be described in Lewis terms
choices.why: This heterodimer is the example the section gives of π stacking readily described as a Lewis acid-base interaction.

choices.text: Both rings equally, since they are the same shape
choices.why: The F substituents reverse the ring's polarity, so the two rings play opposite roles.

explanation: With electronegative substituents the polarity of the ring system is reversed, so an eclipsed heterodimer of benzene and hexafluorobenzene has favorable electrostatic interactions. The relatively electron-rich benzene π system acts as a Lewis base in donating to the electron-poor hexafluorobenzene π system.

prompt: Why are hydrogen bonds considered more than a special kind of dipole-dipole interaction?

choices.text: They are much stronger (~12–20 kJ/mol vs. <4 kJ/mol for typical dipole-dipole interactions) and tend toward a linear D–H···A geometry, reflecting covalent and other contributions
They are weaker than dipole-dipole interactions and have no preferred direction
choices.why: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than typical dipole-dipole interactions and often prefer a linear arrangement.

choices.text: They are full covalent bonds identical to the D–H bond
choices.why: Hydrogen bonds include covalent contributions but are much weaker than ordinary covalent bonds.

choices.text: They only involve dispersion forces
choices.why: Dispersion is one contribution, along with dipole-dipole interactions, covalent bonding, and X-H π interactions.

explanation: Classical hydrogen bonds such as those between water molecules have strengths of ~12–20 kJ/mol, much greater than typical dipole-dipole interactions (<4 kJ/mol), and the O–H···O axis tends to be linear. Hydrogen bonds involve a combination of dipole-dipole interactions, covalent bonding, dispersion forces, and X-H π interactions, in proportions that vary from system to system.

prompt: How does the Lewis acid-base view describe a hydrogen bond D–H···A, and what advantage does it have over the classical definition?

choices.text: D–H acts as a Lewis acid and A as a Lewis base; this view also covers C–H donors and π-system acceptors, which the classical definition excludes
D–H acts as a Lewis base and A as a Lewis acid; it restricts hydrogen bonds to N, O, and F
choices.why: The roles are reversed: D–H offers an electron-deficient H and A donates its lone pair. The Lewis view broadens the definition.

choices.text: A transfers H^+ completely to D; it applies only in water
choices.why: In the Lewis view H is shared between D and A in an adduct, and it isn't limited to water.

choices.text: Both D and A act as Lewis acids; it explains why hydrogen bonds are purely electrostatic
choices.why: A uses its lone pair as a Lewis base. The Lewis view is useful precisely because it accommodates covalent contributions.

explanation: Classically, hydrogen bonds form between D–H and :A, with D and A = N, O, F, and sometimes S. In Lewis terms, D–H acts as a Lewis acid in donating an electron-deficient H, and A acts as a Lewis base. This view takes in hydrogen bonds recognized since the 1990s, such as multicenter H-bonds, C–H, P–H and Au–H donors, and π-system acceptors, and explains covalent contributions through frontier orbitals.

prompt: In [F–H–F]^−, the H sits midway between the two F atoms. What kind of hydrogen bond is this, and how does it compare in strength with asymmetric ones?

choices.text: A symmetric hydrogen bond, which is generally stronger and more stable than asymmetric ones
An asymmetric hydrogen bond, which is generally the strongest kind
choices.why: When D and A are of equal or similar energy, H is centered and the bond is symmetric. Symmetric H-bonds are generally the stronger ones.

choices.text: A symmetric hydrogen bond, which is generally weaker than asymmetric ones
choices.why: It is symmetric, but symmetric hydrogen bonds are generally stronger, not weaker.

choices.text: Not a hydrogen bond, since the donor can't be identified
choices.why: It is a hydrogen bond. Being unable to tell donor from acceptor is what makes it symmetric.

explanation: In asymmetric hydrogen bonds the D–H bond is shorter and more stabilized than the A–H interaction. When D and A are of equal or similar energy, H is centered between them and donor and acceptor can't be told apart. These are symmetric H-bonds, like [F–H–F]^−, and they are generally stronger and more stable than asymmetric ones.

prompt: In Gilli's pKa slide rule, a hydrogen bond is characterized by ΔpKa, the difference between the pKa of the donor D–H and the pKa of the protonated acceptor H–A^+. A donor has pKa 9.8 and the protonated acceptor has pKa 4.6. What is ΔpKa?
explanation: ΔpKa = pKa(D–H) − pKa(H–A^+) = 9.8 − 4.6 = 5.2. That falls in Gilli's 3–11 range, a medium-strong hydrogen bond (6.8–11.5 kcal/mol).

prompt: According to Gilli's criteria, which donor/acceptor pair should form the strongest hydrogen bond?

choices.text: Donor pKa 7.0 and protonated acceptor pKa 6.5 (ΔpKa = 0.5)
Donor pKa 15.0 and protonated acceptor pKa 2.0 (ΔpKa = 13)
choices.why: ΔpKa = 13 falls in the 11–21 range, a medium hydrogen bond. The strongest bonds have ΔpKa near 0.

choices.text: Donor pKa 35 and protonated acceptor pKa 0 (ΔpKa = 35)
choices.why: ΔpKa > 31 marks a weak hydrogen bond. When the donor is far more basic, little H^+ transfer occurs.

choices.text: Donor pKa 12.0 and protonated acceptor pKa 5.0 (ΔpKa = 7)
choices.why: ΔpKa = 7 gives a medium-strong bond. A ΔpKa of 0–3 gives the strong category.

explanation: In Gilli's approach, the pKa values of the donor and protonated acceptor are proxies for each side's pull on the H. When they are about equal, the H is shared roughly equally in a symmetric, strong H-bond. Gilli's criteria rate ΔpKa = 0–3 as strong (11.5–15.8 kcal/mol), down to ΔpKa > 31 as weak (1.1–2.5 kcal/mol).

prompt: In the IR spectrum, what is taken as evidence that a D–H group is hydrogen bonded?

choices.text: The D–H stretching band shifts to lower wavenumber and becomes broader and more intense
The D–H band shifts to higher wavenumber because the bond gets stronger
choices.why: Hydrogen bonding weakens the D–H bond, so its stretch shifts to lower wavenumbers (a redshift).

choices.text: The D–H band disappears completely
choices.why: The band is still present, shifted to lower wavenumber, broadened, and intensified.

choices.text: The D–H band becomes sharper and weaker
choices.why: Hydrogen-bonded D–H bands broaden and intensify.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding weakens the D–H bond, so its vibrational band is redshifted to lower wavenumber, and the band also broadens and intensifies. For example, the N–H stretch of N-ferrocenylisonicotinamide is at 3430 cm^−1 in dilute solution but shifts to 3307 cm^−1 in the solid, where the molecules form hydrogen-bonded chains.

prompt: Which crystallographic observation is evidence that a D–H···A contact is a hydrogen bond?

choices.text: The D···A distance is shorter than expected from the van der Waals surfaces of D and A
The D···A distance is longer than the sum of the van der Waals radii
choices.why: A contact longer than the van der Waals distance is not a bonding interaction. Hydrogen bonds pull D and A closer than that.

choices.text: The D–H bond is shorter than in non-hydrogen-bonded D–H groups
choices.why: Hydrogen bonding weakens and lengthens the D–H bond, when the H can be located.

choices.text: The D–H···A angle is close to 90°
choices.why: Unconstrained two-center hydrogen bonds approach linearity (180°), as VSEPR would predict for a D:H:A unit.

explanation: In crystal structures, hydrogen bonds are distinguished from van der Waals contacts because the D···A distance is shorter than the van der Waals surfaces predict, the D–H distance (when H can be located) is longer than in non-hydrogen-bonded D–H groups, and the D–H···A angle approaches linearity. In the ^1H NMR spectrum, the donor H is deshielded and shifted downfield.
